consensus_summary: The lamb primarily symbolizes Jesus Christ as the innocent, atoning sacrifice (the Lamb of God), with a secondary but common usage referring to God's people or believers as vulnerable members of a flock.
book_summary: A lamb symbolizes a covenant person (one of the flock) and does not by itself mean Christ. Christ is specifically 'the Lamb of God'—the perfect, unblemished covenant person taken from among the flock.
consensus_core_identification: Jesus Christ as the sacrificial offering.
book_core_identification: A covenant person; with Christ as the ultimate, perfect instance (the Lamb of God).
boundary_disagreement: The book explicitly denies that the unmodified term 'lamb' defaults to Christ, requiring context or the title 'Lamb of God' to denote Him. The consensus treats 'Lamb' as inherently and primarily Christological.
material_contradiction: None regarding the referents themselves. Both identify Christ and believers as lambs in scripture, but the book structurally shifts the core definition: it elevates the secondary consensus meaning (a believer/member of the flock) to the base definition, treating Christ as a specific, perfect subset of that category.
rationale: The book and consensus agree on all cases (Christ, the disciples, Jeremiah, etc.), but the book refines the symbol's mechanics. It argues that 'lamb' fundamentally means 'a covenant person,' correcting the common assumption that the symbol points solely or primarily to Christ unless specified.
strongest_objection: The consensus might argue that the New Testament usage of 'Lamb' (especially in Revelation) functionally transforms the symbol into a near-exclusive Christological title, making the book's insistence on 'not by itself Christ' overly pedantic regarding Old Testament usage.
